content: The primary objective of enteral nutrition (EN) is to address malnutrition and improve clinical outcomes. However, EN can lead to complications such as vomiting or aspiration pneumonia, particularly in cases of gastrointestinal dysfunction. To mitigate these risks, many intensive care units (ICUs) recommend monitoring gastric residual volume (GRV). This involves periodically measuring GRV and adjusting the rate of enteral feeding accordingly. Despite its widespread use, there is insufficient high-quality evidence to confirm that GRV monitoring effectively reduces complications associated with EN. Furthermore, the optimal protocol for GRV monitoring remains unclear, and its precise efficacy and safety have yet to be definitively established. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of GRV monitoring during EN, a systematic review was conducted. Electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, were searched for relevant studies up to May 3, 2021. Additional information was obtained by reviewing reference lists of included studies and consulting experts in the field. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), randomized cross-over trials, and cluster-RCTs that investigated the effects of GRV monitoring during EN. No language restrictions were applied. Two independent reviewers screened the search results and extracted data from eligible studies, including details on study design, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. The risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane's risk of bias tool, and the overall certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. A random-effects model was employed for quantitative synthesis, with risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) calculated alongside 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review included eight RCTs involving a total of 1,585 participants, all conducted in ICU settings. Two studies (417 participants) compared less-frequent GRV monitoring (less than every eight hours) with more-frequent monitoring (every eight hours or more). The evidence was of very low certainty and did not provide conclusive results regarding the impact of frequent GRV monitoring on mortality (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.37), pneumonia incidence (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.83), hospital length of stay (MD 2.00 days, 95% CI –2.15 to 6.15), or vomiting incidence (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.09). Two studies (500 participants) compared no GRV monitoring with frequent monitoring (every 12 hours or less). Again, the evidence was of very low certainty and did not provide definitive conclusions regarding the effect of no GRV monitoring on mortality (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.23), pneumonia incidence (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.13), hospital length of stay (MD –1.53 days, 95% CI –4.47 to 1.40), or vomiting incidence (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.93). One study (322 participants) examined the impact of a GRV threshold of 500 mL per six hours on clinical outcomes. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effect of this threshold on mortality (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.38), pneumonia incidence (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.46), and hospital length of stay (MD –0.90 days, 95% CI –2.60 to 4.40). Two studies (140 participants) investigated the effects of returning versus discarding aspirated or drained GRV. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the impact of these practices on vomiting incidence (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.06 to 15.63) and the volume of aspirated stomach contents (MD –7.30 mL, 95% CI –26.67 to 12.06). No studies were identified that compared protocol-based EN strategies incorporating GRV-related criteria with strategies that did not include such criteria. In conclusion, the available evidence is of very low certainty and does not provide clear guidance on the impact of GRV monitoring on clinical outcomes such as mortality, pneumonia, vomiting, or hospital length of stay. Further high-quality research is needed to determine the efficacy and safety of GRV monitoring during EN.
